questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Jordan has earned income and wants to open a Roth IRA. Which action would be a reasonable first step?

choices.text: Apply for a home mortgage.
Request an IRA directly from the Social Security Administration.
Compare eligible financial institutions offering Roth IRAs.
Apply for a credit card.

questions.correct_answer: Compare eligible financial institutions offering Roth IRAs.
questions.intro: Roth IRAs are opened at financial institutions, such as brokerage firms, banks, credit unions, and online investment services. Each provider sets its own fees, account minimums, and investment choices, so the first step is comparing providers that offer Roth IRAs.
questions.feedback: Comparing providers comes first; the government does not open IRAs for individuals.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which type of institution commonly offers Roth IRAs with a wide choice of investments?

choices.text: A brokerage firm such as Fidelity, Charles Schwab, or Vanguard
The Social Security Administration's local field office downtown
A credit bureau such as Experian
A payroll company that prints paychecks

questions.correct_answer: A brokerage firm such as Fidelity, Charles Schwab, or Vanguard
questions.intro: Many providers offer IRAs: brokerage firms (wide investment choice), banks and credit unions (often CDs and savings), and automated investment services ("robo-advisors"). Naming firms is not an endorsement.
questions.feedback: Brokerage firms commonly offer IRAs with many investment options.

misconceptions.C: Credit bureaus do not hold accounts

sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Provider A charges no account fee and offers index funds with 0.05% expense ratios. Provider B charges a $30 yearly account fee and offers funds with 0.60% expense ratios. For a $3,000 Roth IRA, about how much more does Provider B cost per year?
questions.intro: Comparing providers means adding all yearly costs: account fees plus fund expenses (amount × expense ratio).

misconceptions.B: Counts only the fund cost difference

sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which information is generally needed to open a Roth IRA?

choices.text: A home mortgage statement and car title
A credit card and its PIN
A list of every past purchase
Name, address, date of birth, Social Security number, and employment details

questions.correct_answer: Name, address, date of birth, Social Security number, and employment details
questions.intro: IRA applications collect identity and tax information, like other investment accounts. Many also ask you to name beneficiaries, the people who would receive the account if you die.
questions.feedback: Identity and tax information are required; beneficiaries are named too.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: On a provider's website, Jordan sees choices: "Individual brokerage account," "Traditional IRA," "Roth IRA," and "529 college plan." Which should he select?

choices.text: Individual brokerage account
Roth IRA
Traditional IRA
529 college plan

questions.intro: Choosing the correct account type matters: the tax rules attach to the account, not to the investments in it.
questions.feedback: Only the "Roth IRA" account type gives Roth tax treatment.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

sections.relationship: Opening a Roth IRA requires knowing it is an account type, not an investment or a government program.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: An IRA is best described as…

choices.text: a single investment, like one stock
a government payment program
an account type that holds investments with special tax rules
a loan for retirement

questions.correct_answer: an account type that holds investments with special tax rules
questions.intro: An IRA is like a container. The container has tax rules; inside it, you choose investments such as funds, stocks, or bonds.
questions.feedback: The IRA is the container; investments go inside it.

misconceptions.A: Confuses the account with what it holds

sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Who opens a Roth IRA?

choices.text: The government, which opens one automatically at age 18
The individual, at a financial institution
Every employer, for all workers
A credit bureau, after a credit check

questions.correct_answer: The individual, at a financial institution
questions.intro: IRAs are opened by individuals (or by a custodian for a minor) at financial institutions.
questions.feedback: Individuals open IRAs at banks, brokers, or similar providers.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.prompt: A Roth IRA can hold which of these?

choices.text: Stock and bond index funds
A car title
A deed to the house you live in
A debit card

questions.intro: IRAs can hold many investments: stocks, bonds, funds, CDs, and cash.
questions.feedback: Funds are common IRA investments.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.prompt: What does the word "Roth" tell you about an IRA?

choices.text: That it holds only government bonds
That it is insured by the FDIC
That it pays a fixed interest rate

questions.correct_answer: Its tax treatment: after-tax contributions, tax-free qualified withdrawals
questions.intro: "Roth" names a tax treatment (from the senator who proposed it), not an investment.
questions.feedback: "Roth" describes how the account is taxed.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Put the Roth IRA steps in order: (1) fund the account, (2) choose an investment, (3) open the account, (4) compare providers.
questions.intro: Opening a Roth IRA follows an order: compare providers, open the account (identity checks), link a bank and fund it, then choose and buy investments, then check that everything posted correctly.
questions.feedback: Compare → open → fund → invest.

misconceptions.A: Opens before comparing; invests before funding

sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Jordan links his checking account to his new Roth IRA. What does the provider usually do to confirm the link?

choices.text: Asks for his debit card PIN and online banking password by email
Calls his employer
Sends small test deposits or uses secure bank verification
Requires a paper check mailed to the IRS

questions.correct_answer: Sends small test deposits or uses secure bank verification
questions.intro: Providers verify a linked bank account securely, for example with two small "micro-deposits" you confirm, or through a secure bank login service. No legitimate provider asks for a PIN.
questions.feedback: Micro-deposits or secure verification confirm the link.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: When contributing, the form asks which tax year the contribution is for. It is March 2027. Jordan wants to count it toward 2026 and has not yet contributed for that year. Is that allowed?

choices.text: No, contributions always count for the current calendar year
Only if he files for an extension
Only for contributions over $5,000
Yes, until the April 2027 tax deadline

questions.correct_answer: Yes, until the April 2027 tax deadline
questions.intro: Between January 1 and the tax deadline, IRA contributions can be designated for the previous tax year or the current one.
questions.feedback: Prior-year contributions are allowed until the tax-filing deadline (not extensions).

misconceptions.B: Extensions do not extend the deadline

sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.prompt: A few days after buying a fund, what should Jordan check in his account?

choices.text: Nothing; accounts never contain errors
His credit score, which trades affect
Whether the IRS approved the trade
That the purchase shows the right fund, amount, and price

questions.correct_answer: That the purchase shows the right fund, amount, and price
questions.intro: Verifying transactions catches errors early: confirm deposits posted and purchases show the right investment and amount.
questions.feedback: Checking confirmations catches mistakes early.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Why name a beneficiary on a Roth IRA?

choices.text: It lets the beneficiary withdraw money from it right now
It doubles the contribution limit
It says who receives the account if the owner dies
It is required to buy investments

questions.correct_answer: It says who receives the account if the owner dies
questions.intro: A beneficiary designation tells the provider who inherits the account. It usually overrides a will for that account.
questions.feedback: Beneficiary designations direct who inherits the account.

misconceptions.A: Confuses a beneficiary with an owner

sections.skill: Keeping the account safe and organized

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which security step is MOST important for an online Roth IRA account?

choices.text: Turning on multi-factor authentication
Using the same password as on social media
Saving the password on a shared computer
Sharing the login with a friend

questions.intro: Retirement accounts can hold large balances, so protect them with strong unique passwords and multi-factor authentication.
questions.feedback: Multi-factor authentication blocks most account takeovers.
sources: IRS (Individual retirement arrangements): IRAs are set up with banks, brokerage firms, and other financial institutions; contributions for a year may be made until the tax return due date. (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/individual-retirement-arrangements-iras)

questions.prompt: An email says, "Your IRA is locked — log in here to fix it," with a link. What should Jordan do?

choices.text: Click the link and log in quickly
Go to the provider's site directly, not through the link
Reply with his password
Forward it to friends

questions.correct_answer: Go to the provider's site directly, not through the link
questions.intro: Phishing emails imitate real companies to steal logins.
questions.feedback: Typing the address yourself avoids phishing sites.

questions.prompt: Jordan keeps a simple record: date, amount, and tax year of each Roth contribution. Why is this especially useful for a Roth IRA?

choices.text: It shows how much can be withdrawn later as contributions
It raises his contribution limit
It is required to buy funds inside the IRA
It proves he paid tax on the earnings

questions.correct_answer: It shows how much can be withdrawn later as contributions
questions.intro: Roth contributions (not earnings) can be withdrawn any time without tax or penalty, so knowing your total contributions matters.
questions.feedback: Tracking contributions shows what can come out tax- and penalty-free.

questions.prompt: Jordan opens a Roth IRA at a provider that charges no account fee. Over 40 years, how much does avoiding a $25 yearly fee save (not counting growth)?
questions.intro: Total fees over a period = yearly fee × number of years.
questions.feedback: $25 × 40 = $1,000, and more counting lost growth.
